Method Selection Guide

Source: vignettes/method-selection-guide.Rmd
method-selection-guide.Rmd

This package provides more than a dozen alignment methods. Choosing the right one depends on the structure of your problem, not on a single accuracy leaderboard. This article walks through the decision space and connects each branch to the method (or methods) that the current benchmarks support.

The four questions that matter

Before looking at any method, answer these about your data:

  1. Correspondences – Do you know which rows in domain A match which rows in domain B?

    • Exact: row IDs are shared across all domains (e.g. same subjects, same voxels).
    • Partial anchors: a subset of rows are matched; the rest are unmatched.
    • Labels only: you know class/condition labels but not row-level correspondences.
    • None: fully unsupervised.

  2. Overlap – Do all domains observe the same set of entities?

    • Full: every entity appears in every domain.
    • Partial / open-set: some entities are private to a single domain.

  3. Number of domains – Two, or three-or-more?

  4. Output needed – Do you need a shared latent embedding, a linear transform you can apply to new data, or an explicit sample-to-sample transport plan?

The table and flowchart below map combinations of these answers to recommended methods.

Decision flowchart

The flowchart below is a text rendering of the decision tree. Start at the top and follow the branch that matches your problem.

Do you have exact row-level correspondences across domains?
│
├─ YES
│  │
│  ├─ Is overlap full (every entity in every domain)?
│  │  │
│  │  ├─ YES
│  │  │  │
│  │  │  ├─ Do feature dimensions match across domains?
│  │  │  │  ├─ YES ──► generalized_procrustes (simple baseline)
│  │  │  │  │         then try global_geo_align (benchmark leader)
│  │  │  │  └─ NO ───► global_geo_align (benchmark leader)
│  │  │  │             or ssma_align / spectral_mnn_align
│  │  │  │
│  │  │  └─ Do you want multiscale decomposition?
│  │  │     ├─ YES ──► multiscale_manifold_align (research family)
│  │  │     └─ NO ───► global_geo_align
│  │  │
│  │  └─ NO (partial / open-set overlap)
│  │     └──────────► spectral_mnn_align (benchmark leader here)
│  │
│  └─ 3+ domains needing joint consensus?
│     └──────────► coupled_diagonalization or cone_align_multiple
│
├─ PARTIAL ANCHORS (some rows matched, others not)
│  │
│  ├─ Are anchors sparse / noisy?
│  │  ├─ YES ──► parrot (robust to anchor noise)
│  │  └─ NO ───► token_ot_graph_align or grasp
│  │
│  └─ 3+ domains?
│     └──────────► grasp_multiset
│
├─ LABELS ONLY (class/condition but no row IDs)
│  │
│  ├─ Labels clean?
│  │  ├─ YES
│  │  │  ├─ Want speed + simplicity? ──► gpca_align (safest baseline)
│  │  │  ├─ Want latent geometry? ────► kema (linear kernel first)
│  │  │  └─ Hard nonlinear regime? ──► lowrank_align (strongest here)
│  │  │
│  │  └─ NO (noisy / corrupted labels)
│  │     └──────────► gpca_align (most robust to label noise)
│  │
│  └─ 2+ domains with labels?
│     └──────────► gpca_align or lowrank_align via hyperdesign
│
└─ NO CORRESPONDENCES AT ALL (fully unsupervised)
   │
   ├─ Do domains share intrinsic geometry?
   │  ├─ YES ──► gromov_wasserstein or fpgw (structure matching)
   │  └─ NO ───► mma_align_multiple (3+ domains, consensus)
   │
   ├─ Do you have a shared geometry template?
   │  └─ YES ──► multiset_uot_align
   │
   └─ 3+ domains?
      └──────────► mma_align_multiple (consensus baseline)

What the benchmarks say

The package tracks synthetic benchmark results across five fast-profile scenarios that stress different problem axes. The benchmark-guidance vignette has full tables; here is the executive summary. These are frozen historical outputs. Current alignment_method_registry() lifecycle states take precedence over historical rankings.

Takeaways:

  • global_geo_align leads on linear_affine, isometric_curve, hard_nonisometric, and noisy_label_shift with the fastest runtimes.
  • spectral_mnn_align takes over on partial_open_set where it handles unmatched rows gracefully.
  • ssma_align is a strong runner-up on curve and nonlinear regimes.

Label-supervised

Scenario Method Rank Latent cor Centroid acc Runtime (s)
hard_nonisometric lowrank_label 1.833 0.877 1.000 0.017
hard_nonisometric gpca_label 2.833 0.858 1.000 0.021

isometric_curve lowrank_label 2.000 0.890 1.000 0.018

linear_affine kema_linear_label 1.667 0.966 0.983 0.024
linear_affine gpca_label 2.167 0.961 1.000 0.062

noisy_label_shift kema_linear_label 1.667 0.989 0.889 0.021
noisy_label_shift gpca_label 2.000 0.918 0.972 0.022
noisy_label_shift lowrank_label 2.333 0.614 0.833 0.016

Takeaways:

  • gpca_align is the safest label baseline: best on noisy_label_shift, competitive everywhere, and has the lowest seed-to-seed variance.
  • kema with a linear kernel is fast and strong on latent correlation, but more seed-sensitive on curved data. Validate with multiple seeds.
  • lowrank_align is the strongest on the hard nonlinear regime.
  • kema with an RBF kernel is slow and highly variable on these small problems. Use it only when you have reason to believe the kernel is well-calibrated.

Unsupervised multiset and transport

  • mma_align_multiple is the current baseline for 3+ domain consensus alignment with no side information.
  • multiset_uot_align occupies a separate regime: it requires a shared geometry template but achieves very high latent correlation when one is available.

These methods receive no correspondences at all — they discover alignment purely from graph structure. cone_align uses iterative Procrustes on spectral embeddings; grasp uses diffusion-based descriptors. Both run on the first two views of each scenario.

parrot receives 50% of shared row IDs as anchors (the rest are hidden). This simulates the common real-world case where only a subset of correspondences are known.

Methods not yet in the synthetic benchmark

The benchmark now covers the major method families. The remaining gaps are:

Method Why not benchmarked Integration difficulty
grasp_multiset Multiset consensus; needs 3+ domain scenario integration Medium – needs multiset scenario harness
fpgw Pairwise OT; returns transport plan, needs embedding extraction Medium – need to extract embedding from transport plan
gromov_wasserstein Returns transport plan / barycentric weights, not latent embedding High – output is coupling matrix, not embedding
token_ot_graph_align Pairwise graph OT; needs link specification in benchmark harness Medium – need link specification and embedding extraction
cone_align_multiple Multiset; needs multi-domain scenario integration Medium – needs multiset scenario harness

Recommended next steps for benchmark coverage:

  1. Transport methods: fpgw and token_ot_graph_align both return multiblock_biprojector objects, so embedding extraction should work. The main work is constructing the right input format (cost matrices for FPGW, graph links for token OT).
  2. Pure OT: gromov_wasserstein returns couplings rather than embeddings. Benchmarking it requires either a transport-plan quality metric (e.g. fraction of correct correspondences recovered) or a barycentric projection step to produce comparable embeddings.
  3. Multiset extensions: grasp_multiset and cone_align_multiple need the full 3+ domain scenario infrastructure.

Practical considerations

Speed

From the benchmark timing data on small problems (n = 20–25 per domain):

  • Fastest (< 0.02s): global_geo_align, spectral_mnn_align, ssma_align, kema (linear), mma_align_multiple
  • Moderate (0.02–0.2s): gpca_align, lowrank_align, multiscale variants
  • Slow (> 1s): coupled_diagonalization (~3–4s), kema (RBF, full landmarks, 10–50s on n=25)

For large problems (n > 1000), methods with O(n^3) kernel operations (kema with full landmarks, gromov_wasserstein) will become bottlenecks. Use landmarking / reduced representations where available.

Out-of-sample prediction

Not all methods support applying the learned alignment to new data. Methods that return multiblock_biprojector or projector objects support oos_predict():

  • spectral_mnn_align, ssma_align, global_geo_align
  • gpca_align, lowrank_align, kema
  • grasp, parrot, fpgw, cone_align, token_ot_graph_align

Methods that produce point embeddings only (no projection operator):

  • generalized_procrustes (rotation matrices can be applied manually)
  • mma_align_multiple (consensus is fitted, no general OOS)
  • coupled_diagonalization (fitted embeddings only)
  • gromov_wasserstein (transport plan is sample-specific)
  • multiset_uot_align (template-based mapping via multiset_uot_map)

Interpretability

  • Linear transforms (generalized_procrustes, cone_align, lowrank_align): the alignment is a matrix you can inspect.
  • Spectral embeddings (global_geo_align, spectral_mnn_align, ssma_align, gpca_align): the latent dimensions are eigenvectors of a graph Laplacian or generalized eigenvalue problem.
  • Kernel methods (kema): alignment lives in a kernel-induced feature space; harder to interpret directly.
  • Transport plans (fpgw, gromov_wasserstein, parrot): you get an explicit sample-to-sample correspondence matrix.

Quick-reference decision table

For the impatient, here is the shortest path to a reasonable method:

Your situation Start here Then try
Exact row IDs, full overlap global_geo_align ssma_align
Exact row IDs, partial overlap spectral_mnn_align grasp
Class labels, clean gpca_align kema (linear)
Class labels, noisy gpca_align lowrank_align
Hard nonlinear, labels lowrank_align kema (linear)
No supervision, 3+ domains mma_align_multiple –
No supervision, 2 domains fpgw or gromov_wasserstein grasp
Shared geometry template multiset_uot_align –
Need explicit correspondences parrot or fpgw token_ot_graph_align
Feature dims must match generalized_procrustes cone_align
